strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-known problem (exact 0-1 loss linear classification), which is of genuine interest for the interpretable ML community.

The idea of exploiting the fact that all Cover dichotomies are realized by hyperplanes through D points, and incrementally reusing partial computations across combinations, is a reasonable and somewhat elegant algorithmic idea.
The Haskell implementation is fully specified and, in principle, reproducible/executable, which is commendable for transparency.
A formal correctness argument (Theorem 1 and its supporting lemmas using dual hyperplane arrangements) is attempted, going beyond many heuristic papers in the area.
weaknesses: The central claim -- 'the first, rigorously-proven polynomial time algorithm' for an NP-hard problem -- is significantly overstated. That the optimal 0-1 loss hyperplane can be found among the O(N^D) hyperplanes through D points (i.e., enumerating Cover's dichotomies / cells of a hyperplane arrangement) is essentially folklore in computational geometry and learning theory, and is consistent with (not a refutation of) NP-hardness, which concerns the case where D is unbounded/part of the input. The paper's own cited reference (Edelsbrunner, O'Rourke, Seidel 1986) already describes polynomial-time construction of hyperplane arrangements for fixed dimension. The framing therefore misrepresents the technical contribution's novelty.

The actual new contribution appears to be a modest constant/polynomial-factor speedup (from a naive O(N^{D+1}) enumeration to O(N^D) via incremental updates), which is a much smaller and less significant claim than what is advertised in the abstract, introduction, and conclusion.

Roughly half of the paper is devoted to a tutorial on basic Haskell/functional programming concepts (folds, list comprehensions, currying, point-free style) that, while pedagogically written, dilutes the technical content and is unusual and largely unnecessary for a research contribution at a top-tier venue.

The empirical evaluation is very weak: only 5 small UCI datasets (N up to 748, D up to 6) are used, with no runtime/scalability results for ICE itself, despite runtime being the central claimed contribution (polynomial-time complexity). The paper explicitly states that wall-clock comparisons against BnB and MIP/GLPK solvers were performed, but no such results, tables, or figures are actually included in the paper.

No comparison is given against the most relevant related work (Nguyen and Sanner 2013's direct 0-1 loss optimization, or exact MIP-based approaches) in terms of either accuracy or runtime, despite these being explicitly discussed as points of comparison.

The complexity analysis (O(N^D)) ignores or glosses over the cost of solving each D x D linear system and evaluating N points per configuration, and does not empirically validate the claimed asymptotic behavior with growing N or D.

The formal proof of Theorem 1 in the appendix has looseness and apparent errors (e.g., 'according to Lemma 1 and Lemma 1' -- likely a typo/omission), and some steps (e.g., establishing that an optimal cell's adjacent vertex is also optimal) are argued informally rather than rigorously, undermining confidence in the 'provably exact' claim.

The paper does not discuss or empirically demonstrate behavior on data that is not in 'general position' (ties, coincident points, degenerate configurations), which are common in real datasets and could break the stated theoretical guarantees.

Given O(N^D) growth, the practical applicability of the method to even moderately high-dimensional datasets (D > 10) is essentially nonexistent, a limitation acknowledged only briefly in the conclusion without quantitative discussion.

strengths: Addresses a well-known, long-standing problem (exact 0-1 loss linear classification) that is of genuine interest for interpretable ML.
Attempts a formal proof of correctness (Theorem 1) via a computational-geometry/duality argument, going beyond typical 'trust me' algorithm papers.
The idea of enumerating all hyperplanes through D data points (dichotomies) to guarantee finding the globally optimal separator is a clean and understandable geometric insight.
Providing runnable Haskell code alongside the derivation is a nice touch for reproducibility of the core logic, if a reader is willing to engage with functional programming.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated: enumerating all O(N^D) hyperplanes through D points (or equivalently all cells/dichotomies of a hyperplane arrangement) to solve fixed-dimension exact 0-1 loss classification is a classical computational-geometry idea (related to Cover's counting theorem and hyperplane arrangement algorithms cited by the authors themselves, e.g., Edelsbrunner et al. 1986, and prior work by Nguyen & Sanner 2013). The claim to be 'the first, rigorously-proven polynomial time algorithm for this long-standing problem' is not adequately substantiated against this body of prior work, and no complexity or correctness comparison to closely related brute-force/arrangement-based approaches is given.

The stated worst-case complexity of O(N^D) is asserted but never formally derived or proven in the paper; a naive accounting of the described algorithm (O(N^D) combinations × O(N) loss evaluation per combination) suggests O(N^{D+1}), which is the same order the authors attribute to their own earlier, allegedly inferior algorithms. This inconsistency is never resolved.

The correctness proof (Appendix A) has notable gaps and rough patches: the key final argument ('we need to prove that one of the adjacent vertices is also the optimal vertex... Then finding an optimal vertex is equivalent to finding an optimal cell') is asserted rather than rigorously proved, lemma numbering/citations contain errors (e.g., 'according to Lemma 1 and Lemma 1'), and several steps rely on informal geometric intuition rather than precise argument.

Empirical evaluation is very weak: only 5 small UCI datasets (N ranging from 80 to 748, D from 3 to 6) are used, with no runtime/scalability analysis, no verification of the claimed polynomial complexity in practice, no comparison to actual exact competitors (MIP/GLPK, branch-and-bound of Nguyen & Sanner) despite these being explicitly mentioned as having been tested 'in previous work' that is not shown here, and no discussion of how quickly performance degrades with D given the exponential dependence on dimension.

A large fraction of the paper (most of Section 2) is devoted to a tutorial on generic functional-programming/SDP concepts (folds, currying, list comprehensions, tupling) that, while pedagogically pleasant, adds bulk without corresponding scientific content; the actual novel algorithmic contribution is comparatively thin once this scaffolding is removed.

The claimed practical usefulness ('good replacement for linear SVMs... for medium-scale N and small D') is not empirically supported with any wall-clock timing results, making it impossible to assess the practical value of the polynomial-time guarantee, which in the worst case still scales as N^D and is only practical for very small D.

Related work coverage is thin: the discussion of prior exact approaches is largely limited to Nguyen and Sanner (2013) and the authors' own unpublished/unreviewed prior algorithms (E01-ICG, etc., referenced only as 'Exact 0-1 loss linear classification algorithms, April 2023' with no proper citation info), leaving open whether other, more directly comparable methods in computational geometry or optimal separating hyperplane literature have already solved this in polynomial time for fixed D.

strengths: Tackles a genuinely important and long-standing problem: exact optimization of the non-convex, non-differentiable 0-1 loss for linear classification, which is of clear interest to the interpretability/high-stakes ML community.

The geometric argument that an optimal 0-1 loss hyperplane can always be found among hyperplanes passing through D of the N data points (Cover's dichotomies / hyperplane arrangement duality) is a clean and correct combinatorial characterization of the solution space, and the paper gives a reasonably detailed (if not fully rigorous) proof sketch in the appendix.
The functional-programming/Haskell derivation is pedagogically clear and the code is compact and (apparently) directly executable, aiding reproducibility of the described algorithm at the code level.
Table 1 empirically confirms the theorem's guarantee that the exact algorithm's 0-1 loss is never worse than that of SVM, logistic regression, or LDA on the small datasets tested.
weaknesses: The central novelty claim -- 'the first, rigorously-proven polynomial time algorithm' -- is overstated: enumerating all O(N^D) candidate hyperplanes defined by D-point subsets (equivalently, cells/vertices of a hyperplane arrangement) is a well-known technique in computational geometry (e.g., topological sweep, cited Edelsbrunner et al. 1986) and has already been used/considered as an exact combinatorial baseline in prior 0-1 loss classification work (e.g., Nguyen and Sanner 2013). The paper does not clearly differentiate its contribution from this known folklore/geometric fact beyond a specific functional-programming implementation.

No formal, rigorous complexity analysis is given for the actual ICE algorithm in the main text; the O(N^D) claim is asserted in prose rather than derived with a careful operation count, and it is unclear how the incremental tupling scheme actually achieves this bound versus the naive O(N^(D+1)).

The empirical evaluation is very weak relative to the paper's central efficiency claims: only classification error is reported (Table 1), and despite discussing wall-clock comparisons against BnB and MIP/GLPK solvers in the text, no actual runtime results, scaling curves, or timing tables are shown anywhere in the paper. The 'efficient' claim in the title is essentially unvalidated empirically.

Datasets used are tiny (N up to 748, D up to 6), so there is no evidence the algorithm is practical for realistic dimensions/sample sizes; the paper acknowledges in future work that current performance is limited to 'medium-scale N and small D,' which undercuts the practical significance of the contribution.

The improvement in 0-1 loss over SVM/logistic regression/LDA shown in Table 1 is somewhat expected/trivial given Theorem 1 (the exact algorithm is guaranteed to be at least as good on training loss), so this experiment mainly validates correctness rather than demonstrating a compelling practical advantage (e.g., no generalization/test-set results, no comparison to other exact/near-exact 0-1 loss methods in terms of solution quality).

The proof of Theorem 1 in the appendix has rough patches (e.g., a duplicated/incorrect lemma reference, informal reasoning about 'adjacent vertices' being optimal) and relies on a general-position assumption that is not discussed with respect to real-world datasets (ties, duplicate points, coincident hyperplanes are common in practice and could break the guarantees).

A large fraction of the paper (Section 2.1-2.2) is devoted to a tutorial on generic Haskell/functional programming concepts (folds, currying, list comprehensions) rather than the core algorithmic or theoretical contribution, which dilutes the scientific content expected at a top-tier AI venue.

The reference list contains an unusual, seemingly self-referential entry ('Exact 0-1 loss linear classification algorithms, April 2023') with no author, which raises questions about proper citation practice and blinding.

The paper references three prior algorithms (E01-ICG, E01-ICG-purge, E01-CE) developed by the same group without correctness proofs, and mentions unpublished 'small-scale experiments' comparing runtimes, but none of this evidence is actually presented, making several of the paper's efficiency and superiority claims unverifiable.

strengths: Provides a formal proof of correctness (via hyperplane arrangement duality and oriented matroid concepts) for an exact combinatorial algorithm for 0-1 loss linear classification, addressing a gap left by prior similar work (e.g., Nguyen and Sanner 2013) that lacked such proofs.
The paper is unusually thorough in exposition, providing complete, directly executable Haskell code alongside derivations, which aids reproducibility and transparency of the algorithm's construction.
Empirical wall-clock run-time scaling closely matches the predicted worst-case polynomial complexity across dimensions D=1..4, providing a sanity check on the theoretical analysis.
Demonstrates a practical pruning technique (approximate upper bound viability filtering) with empirical evidence of substantial run-time reduction while preserving exactness.
Reasonably comprehensive related-work section situating the contribution among exact and approximate classification/clustering/tree-learning algorithms.
weaknesses: Core algorithmic idea—enumerating all hyperplanes through D points via primal-dual duality and selecting the best assignment—is a long-known technique in computational geometry/arrangement theory (e.g., Edelsbrunner et al. 1986) and essentially matches prior work (Nguyen and Sanner 2013); the paper's main novel contribution is largely restricted to a correctness proof and a functional-programming derivation, which is a narrower contribution than claimed ("first... polynomial time, practical algorithm").

The claimed O(N^{D+1}) complexity is actually worse than optimal incremental arrangement-construction algorithms that achieve O(N^D) for the same enumeration task, undermining the "efficient" framing.

Evaluation is very limited in scale: real-world datasets have D between 2 and 6 and N at most 704; synthetic run-time tests go up to only D=4, meaning the practical utility of the algorithm for realistic higher-dimensional problems is not demonstrated.

No empirical comparison against the closest competing exact methods (e.g., MIP/BnB solvers, or Nguyen and Sanner's algorithm) in terms of run-time or solution quality, despite these being the natural baselines for an "exact algorithm" contribution; comparisons are only to approximate surrogate-loss methods (SVM, LR, LDA), for which ICE trivially cannot do worse on training error since it directly minimizes that objective.

Theorem 1 and its proof assume data in "general position," but real-world tabular data (especially with repeated/categorical feature values) frequently violates this assumption; the paper does not discuss how degeneracies are handled in practice, raising doubts about correctness guarantees on the very real datasets used in experiments.

The generalization argument based on Eq. (1) is not rigorous evidence that the exact 0-1 loss minimizer generalizes better than alternative classifiers with different hypothesis complexity/margin properties; the bound is a uniform worst-case bound over the whole hypothesis class, not a per-classifier comparison, so the motivating theoretical claim is somewhat overstated.

The manuscript exposition devotes several pages to Haskell/functional-programming tutorial material that adds limited scientific value; the actual proof of correctness resides in a separate, classical mathematical appendix rather than following from the type system, making the extensive functional-programming framing feel more stylistic than substantive.

There are signs of insufficient proofreading/polish (duplicated paragraph in the introduction, an unresolved "?" citation in the appendix), which raises concerns about overall rigor and care in the submission.

No statistical significance testing or multiple-run variance reporting for the main comparison table (Table 1), and only modest error bars in Table 2, limiting confidence in the empirical superiority claims on small datasets.

strengths: The paper tackles a well-motivated and long-standing problem (exact 0-1 loss linear classification), with a clear articulation of why exactness matters for interpretability and generalization.
The functional-programming (Haskell) derivation of the algorithm is presented transparently, with executable code provided, which aids reproducibility for readers familiar with Haskell.
An attempt at a formal correctness proof using hyperplane arrangement / oriented matroid duality is provided, going beyond typical 'after the fact' justification common in the field.

Empirical runtime scaling experiments (Figure 2) are reasonably consistent with the claimed O(N^{D+1}) worst-case complexity, and the approximate-upper-bound pruning shows practical speedups (Figure 3).
The paper is honest about the exponential dependence on D in the future work / limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The central algorithmic idea -- enumerating all O(N^D) hyperplanes defined by D points and evaluating the 0-1 loss on each -- is a well-known brute-force/combinatorial-geometry approach (already sketched by the authors themselves in the introduction and via Cover's counting theorem), not a genuinely new algorithm. The paper's claim to be 'the first... polynomial time, practical algorithm' overstates the novelty, especially since the authors themselves cite Nguyen and Sanner (2013) as having already proposed an essentially identical polynomial-time combinatorial search algorithm; the only stated difference is the addition of a formal proof, which is itself somewhat informally argued in places (e.g., key steps in the proof of Theorem 1 are asserted with phrases like 'we need to prove that... ' without being rigorously completed, and there is a self-citation typo 'Lemma 1 and Lemder 1').

The worst-case complexity O(N^{D+1}) is exponential in D, severely limiting the scope of applicability to very low dimensions (the experiments only go up to D=6), yet the abstract and framing ('efficient', 'practical', 'polynomial time') do not sufficiently foreground this major caveat.

The 'viability filtering' upper-bound pruning is essentially a restatement of classical branch-and-bound pruning with an approximate upper bound; presenting it as a substantial new acceleration technique overstates its novelty relative to standard BnB methodology already used in prior exact 0-1 loss/exact tree-learning work discussed in Section 4.1.

Evaluation is narrow and unconvincing: only 5 small UCI datasets (N ≤ 704, D ≤ 6) are used, and the paper never compares against the closest related exact baselines (BnB, MIP formulations, or Nguyen and Sanner's algorithm), only against approximate methods (SVM, LR, LDA) that are trivially expected to have worse in-sample 0-1 loss than an exact optimizer. This does not validate whether ICE is actually computationally competitive with other exact approaches, nor whether its practical runtime is superior.

Generalization results are weak evidence for the paper's stated hypothesis: e.g., on the Caesarian dataset, ICE has by far the smallest training error (16.4% vs 27.9-30.3%) but the largest gap to test error (37.5%), suggesting substantial overfitting from exact 0-1 loss minimization without margin control — this arguably undermines rather than supports the VC-dimension/generalization argument made in the introduction, but is not discussed critically.

The out-of-sample prediction procedure uses an ad hoc 'maximum margin representative' of the equivalence class of the exact hyperplane, introduced without justification, evaluation of alternatives, or discussion of its effect on results.

A large portion of the paper (Section 2) is devoted to a tutorial on basic Haskell/functional-programming concepts (currying, foldl, list comprehensions, point-free style) rather than to novel technical contributions or rigorous complexity/proof exposition, which dilutes the scientific content of a research paper.
There are quality/editing issues, including a duplicated paragraph in the introduction ('Hence, in high-stakes applications of ML...') and typographical/reference errors in the appendix proofs.

The paper claims 'exact' solutions but relies on floating-point linear solves (fitw, linearsolve) with an ad hoc numerical tolerance (smalleps = 1e-8) for detecting points on the boundary; no discussion is given of how numerical precision issues could affect the correctness guarantees in practice, which is an important gap given the paper's core claim of provable exactness.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and interpretable-ML-relevant problem: finding the globally optimal (0-1 loss) linear classifier, which is of clear practical and theoretical interest.

Provides a formal correctness proof for the enumeration algorithm using hyperplane arrangement duality and oriented matroid concepts, which is a step beyond prior informal or unproven combinatorial-search approaches (e.g., Nguyen and Sanner, 2013).

Worst-case time complexity O(N^{D+1}) is derived and empirically validated via log-log run-time slope matching for D=1..4 synthetic datasets, giving good internal consistency between theory and implementation.
Demonstrates a practically useful engineering technique (approximate upper-bound viability pruning) that empirically yields large speedups while preserving exactness.

Empirical results on several small UCI datasets show the exact method achieves equal-or-better training and (in most cases) test error than SVM/LR/LDA, supporting the motivating claim that exact optimization can outperform convex surrogates.
Full, directly executable Haskell code is provided, aiding reproducibility of the core algorithm.
weaknesses: The paper's central claim of being the 'first' polynomial-time exact algorithm is overstated: the authors themselves cite Nguyen and Sanner (2013) as having already proposed an essentially identical polynomial-time combinatorial enumeration algorithm, and the O(N^D) dichotomy enumeration idea follows directly from long-established results (Cover 1965; Edelsbrunner et al. 1986, both cited by the authors) on hyperplane arrangement construction. The genuinely new contribution is narrower (a correctness proof and an FP-derived implementation) than the abstract/intro suggest.

Critically, the paper never empirically compares against Nguyen and Sanner's algorithm (the closest prior work) or against MIP/branch-and-bound exact baselines (Tang et al. 2014, Brooks 2011), so the claimed practical advantage over existing exact methods is unsubstantiated.

Experiments are very small-scale: real-world UCI datasets have N ≤ 704 and D ≤ 6, and synthetic run-time experiments go up to only D=4; given the O(N^{D+1}) complexity, this leaves the practical scalability of the method (e.g., to typical feature dimensions of 10-50+) essentially untested and likely infeasible, undermining the 'practical algorithm' framing in the title.

A very large fraction of the paper (Sections 2.1-2.2, roughly 5 pages) is devoted to tutorial-level exposition of basic Haskell/functional-programming concepts (folds, currying, list comprehensions, point-free style) rather than focusing on the core algorithmic and empirical contributions; this significantly dilutes the presentation and makes it hard to extract the actual novel technical content.

The correctness proof in the appendix has some informal/hand-wavy steps (e.g., the final proof of Theorem 1 asserts adjacency/optimality relationships between cells and vertices somewhat loosely, and several supporting lemmas' proofs are terse), so the 'rigorously-proven' claim is only partially delivered.

No discussion or evaluation of memory usage, numerical stability of the linear solves for near-degenerate configurations (data not in exactly general position), or how the algorithm handles ties/degenerate arrangements in practice, despite this being a a real concern for real-world data.

The related-work and framing oversell significance ('long-standing problem', 'first... practical algorithm') without adequately contextualizing how close prior work already came to the same result, weakening the paper's positioning.
